title: Ch1 1.1: What is the Internet? What is a protocol?

questions.q: In the nuts-and-bolts view of the Internet, what are laptops, smartphones, data-center servers and Internet-connected cars collectively called?
questions.explain: Hosts (end systems) are the billions of connected computing devices at the Internet's edge that run network applications.

questions.q: What does a packet switch do?
choices: Runs network applications for end users
Defines the standard format of Internet messages
Forwards packets (chunks of data) toward their destination
Sets the transmission rate of a link
questions.explain: Packet switches forward packets (chunks of data) to each other and to hosts. Routers and switches are the two types.

questions.q: Which of the following are packet switches?
questions.explain: Routers and switches are the two kinds of packet switch. Smartphones and web servers are hosts, and a fiber cable is a communication link.

questions.q: Which of these can be the physical medium of a communication link?
questions.explain: Communication links are built from fiber, copper, radio and satellite. A router is a packet switch, and HTTP is a protocol.

questions.q: What term describes the transmission rate of a communication link?
questions.explain: A link's transmission rate is called its bandwidth.

questions.q: Your home router forwards packets between the laptops in your house and your ISP. Which nuts-and-bolts component is it acting as?
questions.explain: A device that forwards packets toward their destination is acting as a packet switch, not as an end system that runs applications.

questions.q: An Internet-connected refrigerator or energy monitor is a host (end system), just like a laptop or a data-center server.
questions.explain: Any computing device at the network's edge that runs network applications is a host. That includes appliances, security cameras, cars, fitness trackers, and even a web-enabled toaster.

questions.q: In the nuts-and-bolts view, what is a 'network'?
choices: A single communication link between two hosts
A collection of devices, routers and links managed by an organization
A set of rules for exchanging messages
questions.explain: A network is a collection of devices, routers and links that one organization owns and operates, such as a home, enterprise, campus, mobile or ISP network.

questions.q: Why is the Internet described as a 'network of networks'?
choices: It is made of many separately owned and operated networks, such as interconnected ISPs
Every host contains its own small network
A single global ISP owns and runs every network
Each protocol forms its own separate network
questions.explain: The Internet is the interconnection of many independently owned and operated networks (interconnected ISPs, enterprise, home, mobile and content-provider networks).

questions.q: A university's campus network and the regional backbone network that connects it to other campuses are really one network, because both are part of the Internet.
questions.explain: They are separate networks, each owned and operated by a different entity. Because the Internet is built from many such networks, it is called a network of networks.

questions.q: Which of the following are examples of the separately managed networks that make up the Internet?
questions.explain: Enterprise, mobile, home, ISP and content-provider/datacenter networks are all networks. TCP is a protocol, and an RFC is a standards document.

questions.q: Which organization defines Internet standards and Internet protocols? (Name or abbreviation)
questions.explain: The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) defines Internet standards.

questions.q: Internet standards are published as RFCs. What does RFC stand for?
questions.explain: RFC = Request for Comments, the IETF's standards documents.

questions.q: Why does the Internet need a body that defines standards?
choices: To own and operate the routers in the network core
Protocols describe a standard way of doing things, so devices and networks run by different organizations must all follow the same agreed rules
To set the price of bandwidth on each link
To decide which devices may connect as hosts
questions.explain: Protocols govern all communication, so everyone has to agree on them. The IETF defines these standards and publishes them as RFCs.

questions.q: From the services view, what is the Internet?
choices: The routers, switches and links that make up the network
Infrastructure that provides services to applications such as the Web, email, streaming video and games
The people who use online applications
questions.explain: The services view treats the Internet as infrastructure (a platform) that serves applications. Listing the routers, switches and links is the nuts-and-bolts view.

questions.q: What does the Internet's programming interface give distributed applications?
choices: Direct control over every router along a packet's path
A guarantee that every application runs on the same kind of device
'Hooks' that let sending and receiving apps connect to and use the Internet's transport service
The physical media used to build links
questions.explain: The Internet gives distributed applications a programming interface: hooks that let sending and receiving apps connect to and use its transport service.

questions.q: The service options the Internet offers to applications are analogous to which everyday service?
questions.explain: The postal service offers senders different delivery options. In the same way, the Internet's interface offers applications a choice of delivery services.

questions.q: From the services perspective, the Internet's basic job is to deliver information from one point in the network to another. Complex applications are built on top of that service.
questions.explain: Applications at the endpoints can be very sophisticated, but they run on top of a basic infrastructure that delivers packets from one location to another.

questions.q: You say a title into your TV remote and a streaming movie starts playing. Where does most of the sophisticated logic behind this live?
choices: Inside the routers, which interpret movie titles
In the applications running at the endpoints, on top of a basic packet-delivery service
questions.explain: The complexity lives in the applications at the network edge. The Internet underneath only provides the information-delivery service.

questions.q: The nuts-and-bolts view and the services view describe two different networks.
questions.explain: They are two engineering views of the same Internet. One describes its components, and the other describes what it does for applications.

questions.q: Which of the following are applications that use the Internet's services (rather than parts of the Internet's infrastructure)?
questions.explain: Email, games and e-commerce are applications the Internet serves. Routers, fiber links and packet switches are infrastructure components in the nuts-and-bolts view.

questions.q: Which statement defines a network protocol?
choices: Protocols define the physical media and transmission rate of each link
Protocols define which organization owns each network
Protocols define the format and order of messages sent and received among network entities, and the actions taken on message transmission and receipt
Protocols define which applications may run on a host
questions.explain: A protocol defines the format and order of messages exchanged between network entities, and the actions taken when a message is sent or received.

questions.q: According to the definition of a protocol, which of these does a protocol specify?
choices: The order in which messages are sent and received
Actions taken when a message is sent or received
The brand of hardware each device must use
Which ISP a host must connect to
questions.explain: A protocol defines message format, message order, and the actions taken on transmission and receipt. It says nothing about hardware brands or ISP choice.

questions.q: Which of the following are protocols?
questions.explain: HTTP, TCP, IP, Ethernet, WiFi and 4G/5G are all protocols. The IETF is the standards body, and a router is a packet switch.

questions.q: In the Internet, only some communication activity is governed by protocols.
questions.explain: All communication activity in the Internet is governed by protocols. They are everywhere and control how messages are sent and received.

questions.q: A browser fetches a file from a web server. Which ordering of messages matches the protocol exchange?
choices: GET request → TCP connection request → file → TCP connection response
TCP connection request → TCP connection response → GET request for the URL → the file is returned
TCP connection request → GET request → TCP connection response → file
File → GET request → TCP connection response → TCP connection request
questions.explain: First comes the connection phase (TCP connection request, then response). Then comes the request-response phase (GET for the URL, then the file). Message order is part of the protocol.

questions.q: In the human 'Got the time?' protocol, a 'Hi' / 'Hi' exchange comes before the actual question. What plays the same role when a browser fetches a web page?
choices: The TCP connection request and response
questions.explain: Both exchanges start with a greeting or connection phase (Hi/Hi, or the TCP connection request/response). A request-response phase follows (the time and '2:00', or GET and the file).

questions.q: After the TCP connection is set up, what type of HTTP request does the browser send to ask the server for the file at a URL?
questions.explain: The browser sends a GET for the URL, and the server responds with the file.

questions.q: What do human protocols (like asking someone for the time) and network protocols have in common?
choices: Both always involve exactly two messages
Both have rules for the specific messages sent and the specific actions taken when a message is received or another event occurs
Both are written down as RFCs
Both require a router to relay the messages
questions.explain: Both kinds of protocol set rules for which messages are sent and what each party does in response. In network protocols the parties are devices (applications, hosts, routers, switches, links) instead of people.
